content: 1. Breast cancer is often a hormonally sensitive tumor. Some studies have suggested that the use of oral contraceptives may be associated with an increased risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in certain populations of women. However, there remains controversy regarding whether these findings are influenced by differences in sexual behavior or other factors. Despite numerous studies investigating the relationship between oral contraceptive use and breast or cervical cancers, a definitive cause-and-effect relationship has not been established. 2. Benign hepatic adenomas have been associated with oral contraceptive use, although the incidence of these benign tumors is rare in the United States. Indirect calculations estimate the attributable risk to be approximately 3.3 cases per 100,000 users, with the risk increasing after four or more years of use, particularly with higher-dose oral contraceptives. Rupture of benign hepatic adenomas can result in fatal intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Studies from Britain have shown an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in long-term (greater than 8 years) oral contraceptive users. However, these cancers are extremely rare in the United States, with the attributable risk of liver cancer in oral contraceptive users being less than one per million users. 3. Clinical case reports have documented retinal thrombosis associated with oral contraceptive use. If a patient experiences unexplained partial or complete loss of vision, the onset of proptosis or diplopia, papilledema, or retinal vascular lesions, oral contraceptives should be discontinued immediately. 4. Extensive epidemiological studies have found no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy. Most recent studies also do not indicate a teratogenic effect, particularly concerning cardiac anomalies and limb reduction defects, when oral contraceptives are inadvertently taken during early pregnancy. Oral contraceptives should not be used to induce withdrawal bleeding as a test for pregnancy, nor should they be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. If a patient misses two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed schedule, pregnancy should be considered at the time of the first missed period. Oral contraceptive use should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed. 5. Earlier studies reported an increased lifetime relative risk of gallbladder surgery in users of oral contraceptives and estrogens. However, more recent studies suggest that the relative risk of developing gallbladder disease among oral contraceptive users may be minimal. This reduced risk may be related to the use of oral contraceptive formulations containing lower hormonal doses of estrogens and progestogens. 6. Oral contraceptives have been shown to decrease glucose tolerance in a significant percentage of users, an effect directly related to the estrogen dose. Progestogens generally increase insulin secretion and create insulin resistance, with the extent of this effect varying among different progestational agents. In nondiabetic women, oral contraceptives appear to have no effect on fasting blood glucose levels. However, prediabetic and diabetic women should be carefully monitored while taking oral contraceptives. A small proportion of women may experience persistent hypertriglyceridemia while on the pill. Changes in serum triglycerides and lipoprotein levels have also been reported in oral contraceptive users. 7. Women with significant hypertension should not be started on hormonal contraception. Data from the Royal College of General Practitioners and subsequent randomized trials have shown that the incidence of hypertension increases with higher progestational activity and concentrations of progestogens. Women with a history of hypertension, hypertension-related diseases, or renal disease should be encouraged to use alternative methods of contraception. In general, women who develop hypertension during hormonal contraceptive therapy should switch to a non-hormonal contraceptive. If other contraceptive methods are unsuitable, hormonal contraceptive therapy may continue in combination with antihypertensive therapy. 8. The onset or worsening of migraines, or the development of a new pattern of recurrent, persistent, or severe headaches, requires discontinuation of oral contraceptives and evaluation of the underlying cause. 9. Breakthrough bleeding and spotting are sometimes encountered in patients on oral contraceptives, particularly during the first three months of use. If pathology has been excluded, time or a change to another formulation may resolve the issue. In the event of amenorrhea, pregnancy should be ruled out. Some women may experience post-pill amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea, especially if such a condition was pre-existing. 10. Both ectopic and intrauterine pregnancies may occur in cases of contraceptive failure. 11. Serious adverse reactions associated with oral contraceptive use include thrombophlebitis, venous thrombosis with or without embolism, arterial thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, cerebral thrombosis, hypertension, gallbladder disease, and hepatic adenomas or benign liver tumors. There is evidence of an association between oral contraceptive use and mesenteric thrombosis or retinal thrombosis. Other adverse reactions believed to be drug-related include nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal symptoms (such as abdominal cramps and bloating), breakthrough bleeding, spotting, changes in menstrual flow, amenorrhea, temporary infertility after discontinuation, edema, melasma (which may persist), breast changes (tenderness, enlargement, secretion), weight changes (increase or decrease), changes in cervical erosion and secretion, and diminished lactation when given immediately postpartum.
